title: UI Label
description: Interface strings and microcopy — buttons, navigation, status messages, tooltips, error states. These are the highest-volume content type and the most likely to be hardcoded in components. The schema creates a contract between content and frontend.

id.description: The key used in code. Example: label-btn-submit, label-nav-home, label-error-network

language.description: BCP-47 language tag. Examples: en, it, de, es-419, nl-BE

labelType.description: Where in the UI this label appears. Determines character limit and tone expectations.

formality.description: Register of address toward the learner. Determines imperative form and pronoun choice in all target languages. Must be consistent across all UI labels in the same product.

sourceLanguage.description: BCP-47 tag of the language this was adapted from. Omit if this is the source.

sourceId.description: ID of the source label this was adapted from

component.description: Frontend component this label belongs to. Example: QuizCard, ProgressBar

value.description: The display string. For labels with variables, use {variableName} syntax. Example: 'Welcome back, {firstName}'

variables.description: Required when value contains {placeholders}. Documents each variable for translators and frontend developers.

name.description: Must match exactly one {placeholder} in value

description.description: What this variable represents at runtime

example.description: A realistic example value. Helps translators understand word order and gender agreement.

maxLength.description: Maximum character count for any translated string, based on UI layout constraints. Semantics: this limit applies to the static string as written, including any {placeholder} tokens counted as literal characters (e.g. '{firstName}' counts as 11 characters). It does NOT represent the runtime length after variable substitution — a string like 'Welcome back, {firstName}!' may render much longer depending on the actual value. Runtime length enforcement requires UI-level testing. The validator (validate.js) checks static length only and will flag overruns with an explanatory note.

context.description: Required. Where and how this label appears. Critical for translators who cannot see the UI. Example: 'Submit button at the bottom of the quiz card. Appears after the learner has answered all questions.'

culturalNotes.description: Notes about tone or wording assumptions. Example: 'Try Again uses an encouraging tone. In formal-register languages, ensure the imperative does not read as a command.'

localizationFlags.description: Required on every content item. Signals content adaptability before translation begins.

genderSensitive.description: True if the label may require grammatical gender agreement in target languages (IT, ES, FR, DE). Common in labels that include adjectives describing the learner or their work.

expandable.description: True if the UI component can accommodate longer translated strings. German and Dutch labels are often 25–40% longer than English. When false, maxLength is especially important.

culturalReadinessScore.description: Assigned after completing the universal checklist. Sum of five category scores (0–2 each). Required before content can advance to cultural-review stage.

localeReadiness.description: Per-locale review results. Separate from the source readiness score.

content.context: Primary action button on the quiz card. Appears after the learner selects an option. Triggers answer evaluation.
content.culturalNotes: 'Check my answer' is intentionally learner-owned phrasing (my). This first-person framing works in EN/IT/ES but should be reviewed for DE/NL where neutral imperative ('Check answer') is more natural.

variables.name: firstName
variables.description: The learner's first name as entered during registration

content.context: Greeting shown at the top of the learner dashboard on return visits.
content.culturalNotes: First name use in greetings is standard in EN/IT/ES casual register. In DE/NL professional contexts, using first name without formal introduction can feel presumptuous — consider making this configurable or defaulting to a neutral greeting in formal-register languages.
